trial.title: Rhomboid Intercostal Sub-serratus Plane Block Versus External Oblique Intercostal Block in Open Nephrectomy

endpoints.measure: Time of first request of analgesia
endpoints.description: Time of first request of analgesia will be recorded from the end of surgery till first dose of morphine administrated.
Heart rate will be noted immediately on arrival and at 0, 4, 8, 12, 18 and 24 h postoperatively.
Mean arterial blood pressure will be noted immediately on arrival and at 0, 4, 8, 12, 18 and 24 h postoperatively.
Fentanyl 0.5 μg / kg will be given in case of heart rate or mean arterial blood pressure ≥ 20% of the baseline
Intravenous morphine (3 mg) will be provided as rescue of analgesia. The total amount of morphine given in 24 h will be recorded.

Each patient will be instructed about postoperative pain assessment with the numeric rating scale (NRS) score. NRS (0 represents "no pain" while 10 represents "the worst pain imaginable"). NRS will be recorded at 30 minutes, 2,4, 8, 12, 16, 24 hours postoperatively.
Incidence of block related complications such as local anesthetic toxicity, hematoma formation, and pneumothorax will be recorded.

analysis_trace.content: NCT07642193 is a randomized parallel-group trial comparing Rhomboid Intercostal Sub-serratus Plane (RISS) block vs External Oblique Intercostal (EOI) block vs IV morphine control in open nephrectomy. Primary endpoint: time to first analgesia request. Status: RECRUITING with expected completion 2026-12-30.

Adults (≥18 years), ASA II-III, BMI 20-35 kg/m² undergoing open nephrectomy. Exclusions: psychiatric disorders, chronic pain, coagulopathy, severe cardiorespiratory disease. N=90 estimated enrollment.

RISS block targets lateral cutaneous branches of T3-T9 intercostal nerves and long thoracic nerve via dual-plane injection (rhomboid-intercostal and subserratus-intercostal planes). EOI block targets T6-T10 lateral and anterior branches between external oblique and intercostal muscles. Both provide somatic analgesia for upper abdominal/thoracic incisions without sympathetic blockade.

Retrieved evidence: (1) PMC12900245: EOIP meta-analysis (17 RCTs, n=1032) showing SMD -1.32 for 24h opioid reduction, prolonged time to first analgesia vs no block. (2) PMC11781765: RISS vs PECs II in breast surgery—RISS reduced rescue morphine requests vs control (5/23 vs 23/23, p<0.001). (3) Wang et al 2024 (J Pain Res): Continuous RISS vs ICNB in VATS—lower VAS scores at 12-48h. (4) PMC13494908: EOI case series showing effective analgesia with minimal opioids in major abdominal surgery. No direct head-to-head RISS vs EOI RCTs found. Evidence role: indirect_direction for both blocks vs control; mechanism_background for comparison between blocks.

Primary-0 (time to first analgesia): Both regional blocks expected to prolong time vs IV morphine control. EOIP meta-analysis suggests prolonged duration; RISS breast surgery data shows delayed rescue requests. Between-block comparison uncertain—no direct comparative evidence. Secondary endpoints: HR/MAP expected stable with blocks; fentanyl/morphine consumption expected lower with blocks vs control; NRS pain scores expected lower with blocks; complications expected low incidence for both ultrasound-guided blocks.

Both RISS and EOI are superficial plane blocks with favorable safety profile. Risks: local anesthetic toxicity, hematoma, pneumothorax (rare with ultrasound guidance). No sympathetic blockade avoids hypotension/bradycardia risks of neuraxial techniques.

1. Block failure or inadequate spread in obese patients (BMI limit 35). 2. Open nephrectomy incision may extend beyond block dermatomal coverage. 3. No blinding may introduce performance bias. 4. Single-center design limits generalizability.

Based on EOIP meta-analysis showing significant opioid reduction and prolonged analgesia, and RISS RCT showing reduced rescue analgesia vs control, both active blocks predicted superior to IV morphine for primary and secondary endpoints. Direct RISS vs EOI comparison: no reliable evidence—predicted non-inferiority with wide uncertainty.
No head-to-head RCTs comparing RISS vs EOI. No published data on RISS specifically in open nephrectomy. Time-to-first-analgesia numeric estimates unavailable for RISS in this population.
